screens.title: Subnets: Logical Network Divisions
screens.narratorSegment: Let's begin by exploring subnets, a fundamental building block within your Google Cloud VPC network. A subnet, or subnetwork, is essentially a logical division of your VPC's IP address space. Crucially, subnets are regional resources, meaning they are confined to a single region, even though your VPC network itself is global. When you create a subnet, you define its IP address range using CIDR notation, like '10.10.0.0/20'. This specific range is known as the primary IP range. All VM instances and other resources you deploy into this subnet will automatically receive their internal IP addresses from this primary range. This careful allocation ensures that resources within the same subnet can communicate directly using their internal IPs, and resources in different subnets within the same VPC can communicate seamlessly, provided your firewall rules permit. Think of it like dividing a large office building into floors; each floor has its own set of room numbers, but all floors are part of the same building. This segmentation helps organize your network and manage IP addresses efficiently. Subnets: Logical Network Divisions means subnets are regional divisions of a vpc's ip space, enabling organized internal communication and efficient ip management.. In practical terms, understanding how vpcs are segmented into regional ip spaces.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›Subnets: Logical Network Divisions
Core Concept

What is a Subnet?

A subnet (or subnetwork) is a logical division of a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network's IP address space, confined to a single region.

  • •
    Regional Resource: Subnets are always tied to a specific Google Cloud region, unlike global VPCs.
  • •
    IP Address Allocation: When you create a subnet, you define its primary IP address range using CIDR notation (e.g., 10.10.0.0/20).
  • •
    Internal Communication: VM instances and other resources deployed into a subnet receive internal IP addresses from this primary range, enabling direct communication within the subnet and across the VPC.
Key Takeaway

Subnets provide essential network segmentation, allowing for organized IP address management and controlled communication within your VPC.

Analogy

Imagine a VPC as a large university campus. Each subnet is like a specific department building on that campus, located in a particular area (region). All students and faculty within that building (resources) get their office numbers (IP addresses) from that building's designated range.

VPC Network Segmentation

screens.title: Secondary IP Ranges: Enhancing Flexibility
screens.narratorSegment: While the primary IP range handles most resource allocations, Google Cloud subnets also support what are called secondary IP ranges, often referred to as IP aliases. These are incredibly powerful for advanced networking scenarios, particularly when dealing with Kubernetes Engine, or GKE, clusters, or other applications that require multiple IP addresses per network interface. For instance, a GKE cluster leverages secondary IP ranges to provide dedicated IP spaces for its pods and services. This means that your pods and services can have their own distinct IP addresses within the subnet, completely separate from the VM instances that host the GKE nodes. This separation offers significant advantages: it prevents IP address exhaustion for the primary range, provides greater flexibility in network design, and enhances the overall architecture for containerized workloads. You can easily add these secondary ranges either during subnet creation or later using the gcloud CLI or the Cloud Console, giving you granular control over your network's IP allocation. This is a key feature for scalable and complex deployments. content.html:
Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›Secondary IP Ranges
Advanced Networking

What are Secondary IP Ranges?

Secondary IP ranges, also known as IP aliases, are additional CIDR blocks assigned to a subnet, separate from its primary IP range.

  • •
    Specialized Workloads: Primarily used for advanced scenarios like Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters, where pods and services require their own dedicated IP space.
  • •
    IP Exhaustion Prevention: Helps prevent the primary IP range from running out of addresses, especially in large-scale container deployments.
  • •
    Enhanced Flexibility: Allows for more granular network design and segmentation within a single subnet.
Example Command
gcloud compute networks subnets create my-subnet-with-secondary \
  --network=my-custom-vpc \
  --range=10.10.16.0/24 \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --secondary-range=pods=10.10.32.0/20

This command creates a subnet with a primary range and a secondary range named 'pods'.

Key Takeaway

Secondary IP ranges are crucial for modern, containerized applications, providing isolation and scalability for IP management.

Subnet with Secondary IP Ranges
Subnet: us-central1 (10.10.16.0/24)

screens.title: Internal vs. External IP Addresses
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's clarify the two main types of IP addresses you'll encounter with your VM instances: internal and external. Every VM instance in Google Cloud is assigned an internal IP address, which is drawn directly from the primary IP range of its subnet. This internal IP is your resource's private identifier, used exclusively for communication between resources within the same VPC network. Think of it like a private phone number within your company's internal directory. It's not accessible from the outside world. On the other hand, for resources that need to be accessible from the internet, you'll assign an external IP address. This is your resource's public-facing identifier, allowing it to send and receive traffic from anywhere on the internet. It's like having a public phone number that anyone can dial. Understanding this distinction is crucial for designing secure network architectures, as it dictates how your applications interact both privately within your cloud environment and publicly with the outside world. Misunderstanding this can lead to security vulnerabilities or connectivity issues. content.html:
Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›Internal vs. External IPs
IP Address Types

Internal vs. External IP Addresses

Understanding how resources communicate within your VPC and with the public internet.

Internal IP Address

  • •
    Scope: Used for communication within the same VPC network.
  • •
    Source: Allocated from the primary IP range of its subnet.
  • •
    Accessibility: Not directly accessible from the internet.
  • •
    Use Case: Ideal for backend services, database servers, and internal microservices.
Analogy

Like an office extension number, only reachable from within the company network.

External IP Address

  • •
    Scope: Used for communication with the public internet.
  • •
    Source: Assigned to a VM instance or other network services.
  • •
    Accessibility: Publicly routable and accessible from anywhere on the internet.
  • •
    Use Case: Essential for web servers, public APIs, and load balancers.
Analogy

Like a public phone number, reachable by anyone outside the company.

Key Takeaway

Choosing the correct IP address type is fundamental for controlling network access and ensuring the security and functionality of your cloud applications.

screens.title: Ephemeral External IPs: Temporary Public Access
screens.narratorSegment: Now that we understand external IP addresses, let's look at their two forms, starting with ephemeral external IPs. An ephemeral external IP address is, as its name suggests, temporary. It's automatically assigned to a VM instance when it starts up. The key characteristic here is its transient nature: if your VM is stopped and then restarted, or if it's deleted and recreated, that ephemeral IP address will change. This dynamic assignment makes ephemeral IPs generally suitable for development environments, testing workloads, or any scenario where a stable, unchanging public-facing IP address is not critical. For example, if you're spinning up a temporary server to run a batch job, an ephemeral IP is perfectly fine. However, for production applications that rely on a consistent public endpoint, such as a public website with a DNS record pointing to it, an ephemeral IP would be problematic. It would break connectivity every time the VM restarts, leading to service disruptions. Understanding this temporary nature is crucial to avoid unexpected outages in your production environments. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

External IP Details

Ephemeral External IP Addresses

Ephemeral external IP addresses are temporary public IP addresses automatically assigned to VM instances.

  • •
    Dynamic Assignment: Automatically assigned to a VM instance when it starts.
  • •
    Transient Nature: The IP address changes if the VM is stopped and restarted, or if the VM is deleted.
  • •
    Use Cases: Suitable for development, testing, or temporary workloads where a stable public endpoint is not critical.
Scenario

You're running a temporary data processing script on a VM. An ephemeral IP is sufficient because the public address doesn't need to persist across restarts.

Key Takeaway

Ephemeral IPs are cost-effective for non-critical, short-lived tasks but are unsuitable for production services requiring consistent public access.

screens.title: Static External IPs: Stable Public Endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: In contrast to ephemeral IPs, for production applications that demand a stable, unchanging public-facing IP address, you must use a static external IP address. These are permanent IP addresses that you reserve to your Google Cloud project. Once reserved, a static IP remains constant, even if the VM instance it's assigned to is stopped, restarted, or deleted. This consistency is absolutely critical for services that rely on DNS records, firewall configurations, or client connectivity, where a changing IP would cause disruptions. Imagine a public website: if its IP address changed every time the server restarted, users wouldn't be able to find it. Static IPs solve this problem. You can assign a static IP to a VM instance, a load balancer, or other network services, ensuring that your service's public endpoint remains consistent and reliable. The process involves reserving the IP address first, and then associating it with your desired resource. This is a fundamental practice for any production-grade deployment in Google Cloud. Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›Static External IPs
External IP Details

Static External IPs: Stable Public Endpoints

Reserving and assigning permanent public IP addresses for production workloads.

What are Static IPs?

  • •
    Permanent: Reserved to your project and remain constant.
  • •
    Stable Endpoint: Essential for production applications, DNS records, and firewall rules.
  • •
    Resource Assignment: Can be assigned to VMs, load balancers, or other network services.
Example Command
gcloud compute addresses create my-static-ip --region=us-central1

This command reserves a static external IP address in the us-central1 region.

Static IP Assignment Process

1. Reserve IP

gcloud compute addresses create

2. Assign to Resource

gcloud compute instances create --address

Key Takeaway

Static external IPs are indispensable for production services, providing reliability and predictability for public access.

screens.title: VPC Routes: Directing Network Traffic

Routes are essentially the traffic rules for your VPC network; they define the paths that network traffic will take to reach its destination. Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›VPC Routes
Traffic Management

What are VPC Routes?

VPC routes define the paths for network traffic within your VPC network and to external destinations.

  • •
    Traffic Direction: Dictate where network packets should be sent based on their destination IP address.
  • •
    Internal & External: Apply to traffic flowing between subnets, to the internet, or to other connected networks (e.g., via VPN).
  • •
    Next Hop: Each route specifies a 'next hop' – the next destination for the traffic, which could be a gateway, a VPN tunnel, or a VM instance.
Analogy

Think of routes like a GPS system for your network. When a packet wants to go somewhere, the routes tell it the best path to take, guiding it through various 'intersections' (next hops) until it reaches its final destination.

Key Takeaway

Routes are fundamental for controlling network flow, enabling segmentation, and ensuring all resources can communicate as intended.

How Routes Direct Traffic

Source VM

Next Hop

Destination VM

Traffic from a source VM is directed to a 'next hop' based on the route's destination range, eventually reaching the target.

screens.title: Default vs. Custom VPC Routes
screens.narratorSegment: Within your VPC network, you'll encounter two main categories of routes: system-generated default routes and custom static routes. Every VPC network comes with a set of default routes automatically created by Google Cloud. The most notable of these is the default route that directs all traffic destined for '0.0.0.0/0' – essentially, all internet-bound traffic – to the default internet gateway. This ensures your VMs can access the internet right out of the box. However, for more specific or advanced networking needs, you can create custom static routes. These allow you to direct traffic for particular destination ranges to specific next hops, such as an internal load balancer, a VPN tunnel connecting to your on-premises network, or even a VM instance acting as a network appliance like a NAT gateway or a firewall. For example, you might create a custom route to send traffic for a specific private IP range through a VPN tunnel. A common mistake is misconfiguring these custom routes, which can lead to traffic black holes where data simply disappears, or unintended exposure. Always verify your routes in conjunction with your firewall rules to ensure your desired connectivity and security posture are met.

Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›Default vs. Custom Routes
Route Types

Default vs. Custom VPC Routes

Leveraging system-generated and user-defined traffic rules for network control.

Default Routes

  • •
    System-Generated: Automatically created with every VPC network.
  • •
    Internet Gateway: Includes a default route for 0.0.0.0/0 (all traffic) to the default internet gateway.
  • •
    Basic Connectivity: Ensures VMs can communicate within the VPC and reach the internet.
Example

The default route 0.0.0.0/0 directs all outbound traffic to the internet, allowing your VMs to fetch updates or access external APIs.

Custom Static Routes

  • •
    User-Defined: Created to direct traffic to specific destinations.
  • •
    Specific Next Hops: Can point to internal load balancers, VPN tunnels, or VM network appliances.
  • •
    Advanced Control: Essential for network segmentation, hybrid connectivity, and custom traffic flows.
Example Command
gcloud compute routes create my-custom-route \
  --destination-range=192.168.1.0/24 \
  --next-hop-instance=my-nat-instance \
  --next-hop-instance-zone=us-central1-a \
  --network=my-custom-vpc --priority=1000
Key Takeaway

Combine default and custom routes to build a comprehensive and secure network traffic management strategy for your cloud environment.

screens.title: Reserving a Static External IP
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's put our knowledge into practice with a hands-on demonstration. Our first step is to reserve a static external IP address. This is a crucial action for any production workload that needs a consistent public presence. We'll use the gcloud compute addresses create command. Notice how we specify a name for our IP address, my-app-static-ip, and the region, us-central1. The region is important because IP addresses are regional resources. Once this command executes successfully, Google Cloud reserves this IP address specifically for your project. It's now yours to use and will not change unless you explicitly release it. This reservation ensures that even if your VM is stopped or deleted, you retain ownership of that public IP, allowing you to reassign it to a new instance or service without any disruption to your public-facing DNS records or client connections. This is a foundational step for building reliable and publicly accessible applications in Google Cloud. Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›Deploying VM with Static IP
Practical Application

Deploying a VM with a Static IP

Attaching a reserved IP to a new instance and verifying its configuration for public access.

Terminal: gcloud CLI
# Create VM and assign the static IP
gcloud compute instances create my-web-server \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=e2-medium \
  --image-family=debian-11 \
  --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --network=my-custom-vpc \
  --subnet=my-subnet-us-central1 \
  --address=my-app-static-ip \
  --tags=http-server \
  --metadata=startup-script="#! /bin/bash
    sudo apt update
    sudo apt install -y apache2
    echo '<!doctype html><html><body><h1>Hello from my-web-server!</h1></body></html>' | sudo tee /var/www/html/index.html"

# Verify the VM's IP addresses
gcloud compute instances describe my-web-server \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --format='get(networkInterfaces[0].networkIP,networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[0].natIP)'

# Expected Output:
10.10.16.2,34.123.45.67
Command Breakdown
  • •
    gcloud compute instances create: Command to create a new VM instance.
  • •
    --address=my-app-static-ip: Crucial flag to assign the previously reserved static IP.
  • •
    --metadata=startup-script: Installs Apache and creates a simple web page for testing.
  • •
    gcloud compute instances describe --format: Used to extract and display the internal and external IP addresses.
Key Takeaway

Verifying IP assignment after VM creation is a critical step to ensure your resources are correctly configured for both internal and external communication.

Module 4.2›Chapter: Subnets, IP Addresses, and Routes›Inspect Routes & Cleanup
Practical Application

Inspecting VPC Routes and Cleanup

Understanding traffic flow and managing resources responsibly to avoid unnecessary costs.

Terminal: gcloud CLI
# List routes for your VPC network
gcloud compute routes list --filter="network=my-custom-vpc"

# Expected Output (truncated):
NAME                                  NETWORK        DEST_RANGE    NEXT_HOP        PRIORITY
default-route-00c0000000000000        my-custom-vpc  0.0.0.0/0     default-internet-gateway  1000
default-route-10c0000000000000        my-custom-vpc  10.10.16.0/24  my-subnet-us-central1  1000

# Clean up resources (important!)
gcloud compute instances delete my-web-server --zone=us-central1-a -q
gcloud compute addresses delete my-app-static-ip --region=us-central1 -q

# Expected Cleanup Output:
Deleted [my-web-server].
Deleted [my-app-static-ip].
Command Breakdown
  • •
    gcloud compute routes list --filter: Displays routes, filtered by your VPC network.
  • •
    Route Interpretation: Look for DEST_RANGE (destination IP range) and NEXT_HOP (where traffic is sent).
  • •
    gcloud compute instances delete: Removes the VM instance.
  • •
    gcloud compute addresses delete: Releases the static external IP address.
Key Takeaway

Regularly reviewing routes is crucial for network health, and diligent cleanup of unused resources is vital for cost management and security.

Let's begin by exploring subnets, a fundamental building block within your Google Cloud VPC network. A subnet, or subnetwork, is essentially a logical division of your VPC's IP address space. Crucially, subnets are regional resources, meaning they are confined to a single region, even though your VPC network itself is global. When you create a subnet, you define its IP address range using CIDR notation, like '10.10.0.0/20'. This specific range is known as the primary IP range. All VM instances and other resources you deploy into this subnet will automatically receive their internal IP addresses from this primary range. This careful allocation ensures that resources within the same subnet can communicate directly using their internal IPs, and resources in different subnets within the same VPC can communicate seamlessly, provided your firewall rules permit. Think of it like dividing a large office building into floors; each floor has its own set of room numbers, but all floors are part of the same building. This segmentation helps organize your network and manage IP addresses efficiently. Subnets: Logical Network Divisions means subnets are regional divisions of a vpc's ip space, enabling organized internal communication and efficient ip management.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

While the primary IP range handles most resource allocations, Google Cloud subnets also support what are called secondary IP ranges, often referred to as IP aliases. These are incredibly powerful for advanced networking scenarios, particularly when dealing with Kubernetes Engine, or GKE, clusters, or other applications that require multiple IP addresses per network interface. For instance, a GKE cluster leverages secondary IP ranges to provide dedicated IP spaces for its pods and services. Now, let's clarify the two main types of IP addresses you'll encounter with your VM instances: internal and external. Every VM instance in Google Cloud is assigned an internal IP address, which is drawn directly from the primary IP range of its subnet. This internal IP is your resource's private identifier, used exclusively for communication between resources within the same VPC network. Think of it like a private phone number within your company's internal directory. It's not accessible from the outside world. On the other hand, for resources that need to be accessible from the internet, you'll assign an external IP address. This is your resource's public-facing identifier, allowing it to send and receive traffic from anywhere on the internet. It's like having a public phone number that anyone can dial. Understanding this distinction is crucial for designing secure network architectures, as it dictates how your applications interact both privately within your cloud environment and publicly with the outside world. Now that we understand external IP addresses, let's look at their two forms, starting with ephemeral external IPs. An ephemeral external IP address is, as its name suggests, temporary. It's automatically assigned to a VM instance when it starts up. The key characteristic here is its transient nature: if your VM is stopped and then restarted, or if it's deleted and recreated, that ephemeral IP address will change. This dynamic assignment makes ephemeral IPs generally suitable for development environments, testing workloads, or any scenario where a stable, unchanging public-facing IP address is not critical. For example, if you're spinning up a temporary server to run a batch job, an ephemeral IP is perfectly fine. However, for production applications that rely on a consistent public endpoint, such as a public website with a DNS record pointing to it, an ephemeral IP would be problematic. Once reserved, a static IP remains constant, even if the VM instance it's assigned to is stopped, restarted, or deleted. Moving on to another critical networking component, let's discuss VPC routes. Routes are essentially the traffic rules for your VPC network; they define the paths that network traffic will take to reach its destination. This applies to traffic both within your VPC network and to external destinations, like the internet or other networks connected via VPN. Every packet of data traversing your VPC relies on these routes to know where to go. Without proper routing, your resources simply wouldn't be able to communicate. Think of routes as a set of instructions that tell your network, 'If you want to reach this specific IP address range, send the traffic to this particular next hop.' This 'next hop' could be an internet gateway, a VPN tunnel, or even another VM instance acting as a network appliance, such as a NAT gateway or a firewall. Understanding how to configure and manage these routes is fundamental for controlling traffic flow, implementing network segmentation, and enabling hybrid connectivity between your on-premises and cloud environments. Within your VPC network, you'll encounter two main categories of routes: system-generated default routes and custom static routes. Every VPC network comes with a set of default routes automatically created by Google Cloud. The most notable of these is the default route that directs all traffic destined for '0.0.0.0/0' – essentially, all internet-bound traffic – to the default internet gateway. This ensures your VMs can access the internet right out of the box. However, for more specific or advanced networking needs, you can create custom static routes. These allow you to direct traffic for particular destination ranges to specific next hops, such as an internal load balancer, a VPN tunnel connecting to your on-premises network, or even a VM instance acting as a network appliance like a NAT gateway or a firewall. For example, you might create a custom route to send traffic for a specific private IP range through a VPN tunnel. A common mistake is misconfiguring these custom routes, which can lead to traffic black holes where data simply disappears, or unintended exposure. Always verify your routes in conjunction with your firewall rules to ensure your desired connectivity and security posture are met.
